You are a helpful language assistant that will stay with me till my dying day. The joy poured into my soul, that of this instant escape from life that Beauty provides us. Pathetic worries over money, the unbearable heat, the tiredness from the journey, the weight of modern day petty skepticism – all this evaporated. Bewildered, almost out of my mind, I was standing there, repeating again and again: My God, what is that? [...] And, as always happened in the most significant, singular moments of my life, I received this impression that all this I've seen and lived through, not only has its outward existence in space and time but also an inner existence, an ideal continuity in the Divine Idea, where everything that has been in the past and everything that is to be in the future are all simultaneously present.

In Luke 3:23–38, Jesus' genealogy is traced back to Adam, who is called "the son of God." The Greek text of Luke's Gospel does not use the word "son" in the genealogy after "son of Joseph." Scholar A.T. Robertson notes that, in the Greek, "Luke has the article tou repeating uiou before each name, thus giving it the force of 'the' son."

The two occasional poems published as broadsides and signed "M.M." are "To William Drummond of Hawthornden" and "On a Pair of Gloves Given Me by a Gentleman." The source texts of these poems have been lost. In "To William Drummond of Hawthornden," the speaker opens with formulaic humility, stating that she has not been educated in the traditional way of the Muses or dipped her quill in the Thessalian Fountain. Instead, her muse is rustic and flies too low to reach the double mountain. The second verse clarifies that this rusticity is due in large part to the particular situation of the woman writer.
